Data: [TidyTuesday 2026-08-11](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2026/2026-08-11).

A galaxy's nucleus is classified by the ratios between a handful of emission lines, and the diagram those ratios are read off is one of the most reproduced figures in astronomy.
It plots [O III] against [N II], both divided by a hydrogen line to cancel out reddening, and it sorts nuclei into star-forming H II regions, Seyferts, LINERs, and the transition objects that are supposed to be some of each.
That is the left panel, and the thing worth noticing is how badly it does the last of those four jobs.
The transition objects do not sit between the star-forming galaxies and the LINERs on this diagram; they sit inside the LINERs.
No vertical cut anywhere along the axis gets more than 69.5% of the two classes right, and the best one still hands 37 of the 62 transition objects to the wrong side.

Swap one ratio and the picture changes completely.
Against [O I] rather than [N II], the same two classes barely overlap: a single cut at −0.78 separates 151 of the 154, because every LINER in the survey sits above −0.77 and only three transition objects reach that high.
Two ratios of the same four elements, measured on the same spectra of the same galaxies, and one of them carries almost all of the information the other is missing.
The lesson is not that the famous diagram is wrong, but that it is one projection of a classification that was never two-dimensional.

Two cautions, and the first is the larger.
Ho, Filippenko and Sargent defined transition objects partly on [O I]/Hα in the first place, so the right panel is marking its own homework and the 98.1% is a measure of how consistently they applied their own rule, not an independent discovery.
What survives that objection is the left panel: whatever the transition objects are, the diagram everyone draws cannot see them.
The second is that 25 of the 408 classifications are flagged very uncertain, 14 of them LINERs, which is the class the argument leans on hardest.
A further 71 galaxies carry no class at all, one is pure absorption, and six are missing a ratio; none of the 78 are drawn.
Note also that the four columns named `log_oiii_hb`, `log_oi_ha`, `log_nii_ha` and `log_sii_ha` hold the plain ratio rather than its logarithm, so the figure takes the logarithm itself.
